1016.title: Theophany: blessing the waters
1016.hook: Orthodox priests throw a cross into rivers and sea, and swimmers dive for it
1016.howItsDone: On Theophany, Orthodox and other Eastern churches celebrate the Great Blessing of the Waters, in church and often outdoors at a river, lake or sea, where a cross may be thrown in and retrieved by swimmers; families take blessed water home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epiphany, and chalk above the front door. Your line was bless this house. Did you slow down at your door? Day one thousand sixteen.

A crowd packs the edge of a harbor on a January morning. Boys and young men stand along the dock in swim shorts, shivering, eyes fixed on a priest in gold vestments holding up a wooden cross. The choir sings. The priest lifts the cross high and throws it, spinning, out over the water. It lands with a splash, and a split second later the swimmers hit the water after it, churning toward the spot where it went under. One comes up holding it over his head, soaked and grinning, and the crowd cheers. It happens in Greek towns, in Orthodox parishes by rivers and lakes, and on seashores far from Greece. Today, Theophany.
screen: `THE CROSS SPINS OUT OVER THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Theophany means God appearing, God made visible. For Orthodox and other Eastern Christians, this is a great feast of January, and it remembers one scene above all: the baptism of Jesus in the river Jordan. Matthew tells it. In the King James Bible: "And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Look at who is there. The Son standing in the river. The Spirit coming down like a dove. The Father's voice from heaven. Eastern Christians see the Trinity shown in one moment, at a riverbank. That's the theophany. And here's the turn that explains the harbor. Orthodox Christians teach that Jesus didn't go into the Jordan to be made clean. He went in to make the water holy, so that all water, every river, every sea, could carry blessing. So on this day the priest blesses water, in the church and often outdoors, at a river or a lake or the sea. Families carry bottles of it home. They drink a little, sprinkle their rooms with it, keep some for the year. The cross thrown into the harbor is the same idea acted out: the cross goes down into the water, the way Christ went down into the Jordan, and comes back up. The psalm says it in older words: "The voice of the LORD is upon the waters." Western churches remember the baptism of Jesus too, soon after Epiphany. But the Eastern feast takes the water itself and blesses it.
screen: `NOT TO BE CLEANSED, BUT TO BLESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless a glass of water. Pour a glass and set it in front of you. Look at it for a moment. Water you didn't make, that fell as rain somewhere and ran through rivers and pipes to reach you. Hold the glass in both hands. If you pray, you can trace a cross over it, as some Orthodox families do with the water they bring home, and give thanks in your own words or the psalm's: the voice of the Lord is upon the waters. If you don't, simply hold it and be thankful for it. Then drink it slowly. The bell holds the time.
Theophany. God made visible: the Eastern feast of Christ's baptism in the Jordan, when the waters are blessed and the cross is thrown into the sea.
Your line: the waters blessed. Today, every time you drink, wash your hands, or hear rain, let it be a small reminder that water can carry a blessing. Day one thousand sixteen.

screen: `DAY 1016 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PRAYER FOR CHRISTIAN UNITY (18–25 JANUARY).`

1017.title: Prayer for Christian unity (18–25 January)
1017.hook: a week when churches pray for each other
1017.howItsDone: During the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, churches of different traditions hold shared services, swap pulpits or choirs, and include one another by name in their prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Theophany: a cross thrown into cold water, and swimmers diving after it. Your line was the waters blessed. Which water did you notice? Day one thousand seventeen.

On a weeknight in January, a Lutheran pastor reads a prayer out loud, and the name in it belongs to the Catholic parish two streets over. Across town, an Orthodox priest asks God's blessing on a Pentecostal church that meets in a former shop. A Methodist choir sings in a Baptist chapel, and nobody tries to sign anybody up. For one week, churches that disagree about baptism, bishops and bread stop to pray for each other by name. Not to settle the arguments. Just to pray. Behind that week sits a single night, a table, and a prayer Jesus prays for people who will come after his friends. Today, the Prayer for Christian unity.
screen: `A PRAYER WITH ANOTHER CHURCH'S NAME IN IT.`

segments.voice: John's Gospel slows right down on the night before Jesus dies. After the supper, after the long talk with his friends, he looks up and prays, and the whole of chapter seventeen is that prayer. Partway through, he turns from the friends in the room to everyone who will come after them. In the King James Bible: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me." Notice what kind of sentence that is. It isn't a rule. Nobody is ordered to be one. It's a request, made to God, about the friends. Unity here is something Jesus asks for, not something he hands out as homework. And notice the pattern it points to: one the way the Father and the Son are one. Not identical. Not merged into a single shape. Close, and turned toward each other. That's why the week takes the form it does. Churches don't use it to pretend their differences are gone. Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants still hold different views about how the church is ordered, who presides at communion, and what unity would finally look like. Some hope for one visible church. Some think unity already exists underneath the different names. The week doesn't decide between them. It asks each church to pray the prayer Jesus prayed, and to say the other church's name while doing it. Look at the last clause too: that the world may believe. In the prayer, how Christians treat each other is part of how anyone else hears the message at all. A family that only argues is hard to listen to.

Here's the practice: bring to mind a church you've never set foot in. Maybe the one with the unfamiliar name on the corner. A chapel you pass on the bus. A congregation that worships in a language you don't speak. Settle, and breathe. Picture the door, the people going in, someone setting out chairs. If you pray, you can hold that church before God by name, and ask good things for it. If you don't, simply wish it well, the people inside and the work they do. Stay with that one place, the door, the chairs, the people. The bell holds the time.
Prayer for Christian unity. A week when churches that differ pray for one another by name, taking their words from Jesus's prayer the night before he died.
Your line: that they may be one. Today, say one kind, true thing about a church that isn't yours, out loud, to someone. Day one thousand seventeen.

1018.title: St Brigid (1 February)
1018.hook: Irish families weave rush crosses for the spring
1018.howItsDone: In Ireland, families and schools weave Brigid's crosses from rushes or straw around her feast day, often hanging the new cross by the door or in the kitchen and taking down last year's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a week of churches praying for each other by name. Your line was that they may be one. Which church did you hold in mind? Day one thousand eighteen.

A bundle of green rushes lies on a kitchen table, still damp from the ditch where they were pulled. Someone folds one stalk over another, turns the bundle, folds again, and slowly a small square appears in the middle with four arms reaching out. Tie the ends with thread and it's done: a cross that looks a little like a pinwheel. In Ireland, families make these at the start of February and hang them over the door or in the kitchen, and the old one from last year comes down. They aren't carved from wood. They're woven from whatever grows by the field. Behind the custom is a woman, a sickbed, and a story about explaining the faith with what was lying on the floor. Today, St Brigid.

Tradition honors Brigid of Kildare as one of Ireland's patron saints. What's told about her comes from lives of the saint written after her time; the Bible doesn't mention her. The stories paint the kind of person she was: a woman who led a community at Kildare and gave things away, sometimes alarmingly. One story has her handing her father's sword to a poor man so he could sell it for food. The cross comes from another story. Tradition says Brigid was called to the bedside of a dying man, a chieftain who did not share her faith. He was restless and couldn't be calmed. The floor was strewn with rushes, the way floors were then, so she sat down, picked some up, and began to weave a cross while she talked about the man who died on one. The story says he grew quiet, listened, and asked to be baptized before he died. That's the shape of Brigid's faith in the stories: practical, close to the ground, made from whatever was at hand. Not gold, not marble. Rushes from the floor. Her day falls at the hinge of the Irish year, when the worst of winter is turning and the first lambs come. Some readers note that the turn of spring was marked in Ireland before Christianity too, and that Brigid's day gathered up that older season. So the cross over the door carries two hopes at once: the faith she taught, and the plain fact that the light is coming back. The Song of Solomon puts the second hope this way: "For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; The flowers appear on the earth."
screen: `A WOMAN OF KILDARE, KNOWN BY TRADITION.`
`MADE FROM WHAT WAS ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make a simple cross from whatever is near you. Two pencils and a rubber band. Two twigs from outside. A strip of paper folded over another. A pair of drinking straws. Don't worry about making it beautiful. Brigid's was made from the floor. Settle, and breathe, and let your hands do the work slowly. While you make it, think of one thing you are waiting on to turn, the way winter turns. If you pray, you can hold that before God as you finish. Then set your cross somewhere you'll see it. The bell holds the time.
St Brigid. A saint of Kildare, remembered in tradition for generous hands and a cross woven from rushes at a dying man's bed.
Your line: spring is coming. Today, look for one small sign that something is turning, a longer evening, a bud, a thaw, and say it out loud. Day one thousand eighteen.

1019.title: Candlemas (2 February)
1019.hook: forty days after Christmas: Simeon's light, and candles blessed
1019.carry: a light to lighten the gentiles
1019.howItsDone: At Candlemas, Catholic, Anglican and some Lutheran churches bless candles and carry them in procession; Orthodox churches keep the same feast as the Meeting of the Lord, and Simeon's song is sung at evening prayer in several traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Brigid and a cross woven from floor rushes. Your line was spring is coming. What sign of it did you find? Day one thousand nineteen.

Two small birds. That's the offering a young couple come to the temple in Jerusalem to make, along with their baby. The law in Leviticus says that after the birth of a son the mother waits seven days, then thirty-three more, and then brings an offering: a lamb, or, if she can't afford a lamb, two turtledoves or two young pigeons. Mary and Joseph come with the birds' offering. In the crowded courts, one man has been waiting for something only he knows about. Churches keep this day in early February, counting from Christmas, and in some churches it begins with candles. Today's word is what the couple came to do.

Luke tells it like this, in the King James Bible: "And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord." That's the Presentation: a firstborn son brought to the temple and offered back to God, the way the law asks. A family doing what faithful families did. Then Simeon. Luke says he was just and devout, and that the Holy Ghost had shown him he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ. So he has been waiting, scanning faces. And when this couple with their two birds walks in, he knows. He takes the baby in his arms, blesses God, and says words that some churches still sing at the close of the day: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation, Which thou hast prepared before the face of all people; A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel." See what Simeon is holding: a baby who hasn't said a word. And he calls him light, for his own people and for everyone outside them. Light sits at the heart of the English name for the day, Candlemas. In some churches candles are blessed and carried in procession, lit against the February dark, in some places the candles for the year ahead. Orthodox Christians call the feast the Meeting, because the old man and the child meet. Catholics and Anglicans often call it the Presentation. However it's named, Simeon's part of the story ends with a man at peace, ready to go, because he got to hold the light before he left.

Here's the practice: light a candle, if you have one, or switch on one small lamp in a dim room. Settle, and breathe. Look at the flame for a while. Think of something you've waited a long time to see, and whether it came. If you pray, you can say Simeon's words slowly: Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word. If you don't, simply sit with the light and let your shoulders drop, the way someone does when a long wait is over. The bell holds the time.
Presentation. The baby brought to the temple and offered to God, where Simeon took him in his arms and called him a light.
Your line: a light to lighten the gentiles. Today, notice someone standing at the edge of a group near you, and draw them in. Day one thousand nineteen.

1020.title: Shrove Tuesday
1020.hook: confess and use up the rich food before Lent: pancakes
1020.howItsDone: On the Tuesday before Ash Wednesday, families and churches in Britain, Ireland and elsewhere make pancakes, and some parishes hold pancake suppers or races; in other places the same day is kept as Mardi Gras or Carnival.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Candlemas: Simeon holding a baby and calling him light. Your line was a light to lighten the gentiles. Who did you bring a little light to? Day one thousand twenty.

Eggs, butter, milk, a bag of flour, a bit of sugar. On one Tuesday a year, in kitchens across Britain, Ireland and plenty of other places, all of it goes into one bowl and comes out as a stack of pancakes. Lemon and sugar for some, syrup for others, a flip in the pan that lands on the floor at least once. In New Orleans the same day is Mardi Gras, French for fat Tuesday, with parades. It looks like a party, and it is. But the old English name for the day isn't about food at all. It's about the other thing people did before Lent began: they went to church and told the truth about themselves. Today's word is shrove.

To shrive is an old English verb. It means to hear someone's confession and declare them forgiven. Shrove is its old past form, and shriven is what you are afterward: confessed, and let go. So Shrove Tuesday is the day you got shriven, cleared out before the long fast of Lent began the next morning with Ash Wednesday. The letter of James puts the practice of telling your faults to someone else plainly, in the King James Bible: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." Notice the direction there. One to another. Not only up to God, but across, to a person. And the reason given isn't shame. It's healing. Churches practice this differently. Catholics and Orthodox Christians have the sacrament of confession with a priest. Anglicans offer it, and some use it. Some Protestant churches confess together, out loud, in a shared prayer, or between friends. Then the pancakes. Lent was traditionally a time of fasting from rich foods, and in some places that meant eggs, butter and milk. A kitchen full of them on Tuesday night would spoil, or tempt. So you used them up. You cooked everything rich in the house and fed everyone you could. Put the two halves together and the day makes sense. Empty the heart, then empty the pantry. Say what's wrong, then sit down and eat with the people who know. Clearing out and celebrating aren't opposites here. The feast comes after the truth is told.

Here's the practice: a small clearing out. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself, gently, what you'd want to set down before a fresh start. Not a long list. One thing. A sharp word you said. A promise you let slide. Just name it to yourself. If you pray, you can tell it to God plainly and ask to be let go of it. If you don't, simply say it once, honestly, in your own head. Then let your mind turn to food: who could you make pancakes with, or share a meal with, this week? Pick a name. The bell holds the time.
Shrove. The old past form of shrive: to hear a confession and set someone free of it. The day before Lent, named for clearing out the heart.
Your line: shriven and fed. Today, own up to one small thing with the person it touched, and then share some food. Day one thousand twenty.

1021.title: Clean Monday
1021.hook: the Orthodox begin Lent on a Monday with kites, simple food, and forgiveness asked of everyone
1021.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians attend Forgiveness Vespers on the Sunday evening before Lent, where each person asks forgiveness of the others; on Clean Monday they begin the Lenten fast from meat and dairy, and in Greece families often picnic outdoors and fly kites.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shrove Tuesday: the heart cleared out, then the pantry. Your line was shriven and fed. Who did you share food with? Day one thousand twenty-one.

"Forgive me." The words go down a line of people in an Orthodox church on a Sunday evening, one person to the next. The priest bows to the first person in the congregation and asks it. Then that person turns to the next. Old women ask teenagers. Husbands ask wives. Someone asks the neighbor they haven't spoken to since the autumn. By the end, the line has reached everyone. The next morning, in Greece, families drive out to the hills with bread, olives and vegetables, no meat, no cheese, and fly kites against the sky. A day of forgiveness, then a day of wind and plain food. The Orthodox begin Lent on a Monday. Today, Clean Monday.

Yesterday was the Western way into Lent, with confession and pancakes before Ash Wednesday. Orthodox churches keep their own calendar for the season, and their Lent opens a different way: not on a Wednesday but on a Monday, and not with ashes but with a long chain of people asking pardon. The Sunday before is called Forgiveness Sunday. The Gospel read that day includes Jesus's words from the Sermon on the Mount, in the King James Bible: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." So the church takes it literally. Before the fast starts, everyone asks forgiveness of everyone, and the custom is that you ask whether or not you think you did anything wrong. It isn't a trial. Nobody has to prove who started it. The point is to go into the season with nothing owed. Then comes Monday, called clean. Clean in two ways. Clean in the kitchen: the meat and the dairy are gone, and the food turns simple. And clean in the heart, which is why the forgiveness came first. The prophet Isaiah has a line that could hang over the whole day: "Wash you, make you clean." And the kites? Nobody in the Bible flies one. In Greece they're simply part of how families keep the day, outdoors, together, looking up. Some readers like the picture: a season that begins with your eyes lifted, the air clear, the weight a little lighter. A fast that starts on a hillside with the people you just asked to forgive you.

Here's the practice: bring to mind one person you'd ask to forgive you. It doesn't have to be someone you wronged badly. In the Orthodox custom you ask even when you're not sure what you did. A sibling. A coworker. A friend gone quiet. Settle, and breathe. Picture their face. Then, in your own mind, say the two words to them: forgive me. Stay with the words a moment. If you pray, you can bring that person before God. If you don't, just hold them kindly. Then decide whether you'll say it to them for real. The bell holds the time.
Clean Monday. The first day of Lent in Orthodox churches, after a night of everyone asking forgiveness: clean food, clean heart, and kites in the air.
Your line: forgive me. Today, say those two words to one person, out loud, without explaining or defending, and let them answer however they will. Day one thousand twenty-one.

1022.title: Forty days
1022.hook: Moses on the mountain, Elijah on the road, Jesus in the desert
1022.howItsDone: During Lent, Christians often take on a practice for the season, such as fasting, giving something up, extra prayer, or giving to the poor, and churches connect the season to Jesus's forty days in the wilderness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clean Monday, and a line of people asking pardon of each other. Your line was forgive me. Did you say it to someone? Day one thousand twenty-two.

A man alone on a mountain, with no bread and no water, while a cloud rests on the peak. Another man, worn out and wanting to die, asleep under a juniper tree in the desert until someone wakes him and puts food beside his head. A third, just baptized, walking out into the wilderness with nothing. Three different stories, from different parts of the Bible, and the same span of time keeps turning up in all three. Not a week. Not a year. Something long enough to hurt, and long enough to change you. Today, forty days.

Start with Moses. In Exodus he goes up to meet God and stays, and the King James Bible says: "And he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights; he did neither eat bread, nor drink water." He comes down carrying the words of the covenant on stone. Then Elijah. He has run for his life and lain down to die, and an angel brings him bread and water, twice. The text says: "And he arose, and did eat and drink, and went in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb the mount of God." At the end of that road, on that mountain, he hears God not in the wind or the earthquake or the fire, but in a still small voice. And then Jesus. Matthew says: "And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred." Then the tempter comes, and Jesus answers him with words from scripture. Set the three forties side by side. Each one is hard: hunger, exhaustion, testing. Each one is spent close to God, away from the usual noise. And each one ends. Moses comes down. Elijah arrives. Jesus walks out to begin his work. The forty is not a life sentence. It's a passage with a far side. That's why churches link Lent to these stories, and above all to Jesus in the desert: a season long enough for something to shift, and short enough to see the end of. Look back over this week: the waters of Theophany, a week of prayer for unity, Brigid's rushes, Simeon's candle, then pancakes and a line of people saying forgive me. The last two stand at the very door of the forty days.

Here's the practice: choose one thing to keep for forty days. Small enough to actually do. A walk each morning. Ten minutes off the phone before bed. A psalm read each day. One kind message sent each day to someone different. Or giving something up that's been taking too much room. Settle, and breathe. Let a few ideas come and go, and don't grab the first. Then pick one, and picture day forty: what might be different by then. If you pray, you can offer the forty days to God. If you don't, simply hold the choice and let it settle. The bell holds the time.
Forty days. The span of Moses on the mountain, Elijah on the road, and Jesus in the desert. A hard passage, close to God, that comes to an end.
Your line: forty is enough. Today, write down the one thing you chose and the date that's forty days from now. Day one thousand twenty-two.
